title: Merz vows to stay on as chancellor despite ‘disaster’ in another German regional vote
text:
The embattled chancellor’s conservative party suffered its worst result in postwar German history as the far-right AfD won its second regional election in two weeks.

BERLIN — Germany’s embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservatives suffered a second major defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in a regional vote Sunday — a result Merz conceded was a “disaster.”But the chancellor moved to quickly quell a rising storm of speculation that he would move to step aside following the loss, which comes only two weeks after another historic defeat to the AfD in a regional contest. He appeared before cameras just minutes after the polls closed Sunday to say he would continue to push through his reform agenda and act as an anchor of stability in turbulent times.“These reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism,” he said. “What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience. I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country.”The AfD won around 38% of the vote in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the second-best result in its history, just ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) on 35%, according to preliminary results.

Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered its worst result in a state or national election since the end of World War II, by the end of election night coming in at 4.9%, according to a preliminary count, just below the vote threshold required to make it into the state parliament.

The failure to meet that threshold deals an even more painful blow to the chancellor, who is already struggling to maintain support among his party’s rank and file.

AfD leaders hailed their victory — party national co-leader Tino Chrupalla called the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result a “sensation” — while also putting the pressure on a profoundly weakened Merz to step aside and abandon his party’s policy of maintaining a “firewall” around the far right.“Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU and is dragging the CDU down with him,” national co-leader Alice Weidel told German public television. “So the CDU must ask itself, above all else, does it want to continue with this chancellor and with these left-wing policies?”

Merz took the unusual step of convening CDU leaders at the party’s Berlin headquarters on Sunday night in an effort to rally their support ahead of what he knew would be another humiliating election defeat. Merz’s approval ratings are among the lowest ever recorded for a German chancellor at this point in their tenure, prompting internal CDU discussions about a possible change at the top—Kanzlertausch.

“Of course, the mood isn’t exactly lighthearted,” Ines Claus, a CDU politician who took part in the leadership meeting, told ARD. “If you ask me now whether one might prefer to just pull the covers over one’s head, well, that might be the case. But that’s not what responsibility is about; stability is what’s required now.”

Ahead of the election, one CDU official told POLITICO that “all hell breaks loose” in the party if the conservatives fail to make it into Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament — an outcome that remained distinctly possible as of 10 p.m. on election night.

Just 1% of voters — and 1% of CDU supporters — said Chancellor Merz had helped his party’s election performance in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to a poll by public broadcaster ZDF.“We can’t sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania,” Merz said after the polls closed Sunday. “It’s a disaster.”The CDU also saw its support decline in a separate regional vote in Berlin, finishing second with around 19%, according to a preliminary count, behind the Left party, a far-left force which won 25.5% and is now poised to take over the capital’s mayoralty from Merz’s conservatives in coalition with center-left parties.

Merz has staked his chancellorship on a reform agenda he argues will boost Germany’s competitiveness and restore growth to the EU’s largest economy, and has urged voters to be patient as the reforms kick in.

But as Germany’s export-oriented growth model continues to suffer amid increased competition from China and U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff wars, German voters don’t appear to be giving him the benefit of the doubt.

The chancellor’s agenda includes raising the retirement age to shore up the pension system, cutting some health-insurance benefits to curb rising premiums and making it harder for workers to take sick leave in an effort to boost growth.

Many of those reforms impose clear costs on ordinary voters, giving the far right and far left ample opportunity to exploit public discontent.

Despite the AfD’s victory in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the party has no chance of governing in the state in part due to a late, come-from-behind surge for the SPD under state premier Manuela Schwesig, who cast herself in the election as a bulwark against the far right by employing the slogan “Frau gegen Blau” — “Woman against Blue,” a reference to the AfD’s party color.Schwesig is now likely to lead a new coalition government in the state with a coalition of left-wing parties.CDU leaders blamed Schwesig’s approach for effectively turning the election in her state into a two-party race that has greatly weakened Merz’s conservatives. “The CDU fought hard, but in the end, it was crushed in the escalating confrontation between the SPD and the AfD,” Merz said.But Schwesig blamed Merz and the CDU for failing to connect with voters and was able to gain on the AfD late in the race in great part because she attacked Merz as out of touch with ordinary people and his reform drive as punishing some of the most vulnerable.“The issue of the cost of living is a very significant one, and it’s important for the federal government to take a stand in favor of greater economic development to create jobs, but also to provide relief,” she told a public television broadcaster after the vote.

Still, trying to stabilize the situation, Philipp Amthor, a CDU politician from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the chancellery’s federal-state affairs chief, said it was time to end the Kanzlertausch discussion.

“We have seen that what we have experienced over the past two weeks since the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has done more harm than good — namely, ongoing discussions about personnel that have completely overshadowed the discussion of the issues at hand,” he said.

“In that regard, it is right to put an end to these personnel discussions now and refocus on the issues.”

This story has been updated.

But leading German economists warned of more trouble ahead, including rapidly rising debt levels.

Berlin’s Europe minister rebuked the European Council president’s remarks to POLITICO.

Chancellor insists his reforms are needed to revive the economy and competitiveness, but the proposals are turning off voters.

The chancellor is clinging to power, promising a political reset to unite the CDU’s rank and file behind his leadership.
